sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Recently, wearable devices and wireless sensor networks have become widely popular in various areas such as consumer electronics, environmental monitoring condition monitoring, structural health monitoring, intelligent buildings and structures, traffics and implantable medical electronics [1]. Energy harvesting from ambient environment has gained growing attention to replace the traditional batteries due to their limited lifespan, regular replacement and environmental pollution [2]. A variety of available ambient energy sources like vibration, wind, ocean waves, heat, rotation, and human motion are scavenged and converted into useful electric energy [3]. Since the wind is a kind of ubiquitous, abundant and environment-friendly energy source, a number of research groups have focused on wind energy harvesting to provide power for self-powered electronics. Typically, wind energy is converted into electric energy by exploiting three kinds of mechanisms, i.e., electromagnetic effect [4], electrostatic effect [5], and piezoelectric effect [6,7]. Among them, piezoelectric transduction has high power density, high energy conversion efficiency and ease of fabrication and implementation [8,9]. Therefore, piezoelectric wind energy harvesters (PWEHs) by using aerodynamic phenomena such as vortex-induced vibration (VIV) [10], turbulence [11], flutter [12] and wake galloping [13] to produce continuous vibration required for piezoelectric transduction have attracted great interests in recent years. Currently, one of the most extensively explored PWEHs is the VIV-based harvester since it can be easily implemented and activated under the low-speed wind [14].

As is well known, the VIV is caused by periodical vortex shedding from a non-streamlined bluff body like a circular cylinder when the incoming wind flows over the bluff body [15]. Generally, VIV presents a large amplitude and occurs within a narrow wind speed range [16]. In order to harvest wind energy using the VIV effectively, numerous researchers presented various principles and configurations of the VIVbased PWEHs. Barrero-Gil et al. conducted a parametric study of VIV of a circular cylinder to identify the effect of governing parameters on the energy extraction efficiency [17]. Sivadas et al. carried out a preliminary study on harvesting wind energy from piezoelectric transducers by using VIV phenomena. The effect of different bluff-body shapes and dimensions was investigated, including cylinder, triangle, and pentagon [18]. Akaydin et al. proposed a self-excited wind energy harvester whose available power was proportional to the cube of the wind speed, and proved the potential for generating large amounts of electrical energy from the wind energy by exploiting the direct piezoelectric effect [19]. Mehmood et al. investigated the concept of piezoelectric energy harvesting from VIV of a circular cylinder in detail and analyzed the effect of the load resistance on the energy harvester response. The experimental results showed there was an optimal load resistance to maximize the harvested power [20]. Hu et al. expanded the range of aeroelastic instabilities of a cylinder to improve the efficiency of a VIVbased PWEH through attaching two small-diameter cylindrical rods on two sides of the cylinder [21]. Lee et al. focused on the piezoelectric MEMS wind energy harvester placed in multiple cylinders in formation to increase VIV energy harvesting output power. The experimental results indicated that the energy harvester in a cylinder array yielded noticeably higher power output than the harvester using a single cylinder [22]. Wang et al. presented a high-performance PWEH with Yshaped attachments on the cylinder bluff body. The transition from VIV into galloping by adding Y-shaped attachments to the bluff body was verified by experiments [23]. Liu et al. proposed a new method to ivt peoa y la  dble-plastrucuu stream of the circular cylinder in the wind energy harvester. It demonstrated that higher voltage output capability by this method at low wind speed significantly expanded the application scope of wind energy harvesters [24]. Wang et al. proposed a hybrid PWEH with a crosssectioned bluff body to improve the energy harvesting performance by coupling both VIV and galloping phenomena. It exhibited an up to $7 1 \%$ improvement of the maximum voltage output [25]. He et al. took use of the interaction between VIV and galloping to improve the performance of PWEHs. It demonstrated that the interaction between VIV and galloping could reduce the working wind speeds and increase the electrical outputs at low wind speeds [26]. Qin et al. proposed a bi-stable PWEH to increase the harvesting efficiency by introducing the dynammuli-stability and incorporating the meri oVIVandgallping. The bi-stable PwEH could produce a large amplitude vibration over a wide wind speed and enhance the output voltage [27]. Naseer et al. designed an enhanced broadband VIV-based PWEH by introducing nonlinear attractive magnetic forces. The results showed that the efficient and broadband energy harvesting could be obtained by adjusting the PWEH parameters [28]. Zhang et al. explored the improvement of piezoelectric energy harvesting from VIV by using the nonlinear magnetic forces. It demonstrated that the performance and lock-in region of the VIV-based PWEH were greatly enhanced [29]. Wang et al. proposed a cross-coupled dual-beam structure for energy harvesting from VIV induced by wind flows in different directions. A parametric study was performed to reveal the effect of the dimension of the bluff body on the output performance of the novel energy harvester which indicated a potential broadband capability [30]. Nishi et al. put forward a new way for harvesting wind energy by using a vibrating mass inserted between another vibrating mass and generator, which could widen the reduced velocity range with the system excited [31].

A brief survey of literatures shows that the researchers have already conducted lots of work on piezoelectric energy harvesters using the vortex-induced vibrations. And the research domains of vIV-based PWEHs have changed from the energy conversion mechanism [1719] to the improvement of electrical output [22,24], construction of multistability systems [27], the broadband energy harvesting [28,29], construction of multi-degree-of-freedom systems[30,31], the combination of VIV and other wind-induced vibrations [23,25]. Meanwhile, it was also found that the typical configuration, namely the bluff body attached on the free end of piezoelectric cantilever beams, was the most popularly adopted in almost all the VIV-based PWEHs. There is no doubt that the above-mentioned research efforts have greatly promoted the development and performance improvement of the VIV-based PWEHs. Nevertheless, because the piezoelectric beams of PWEHs interacted directly with the wind, it was also very possible to cause some problems, such as poor environmental adaptability, low reliability and wind erosion in long-term use. Moreover, since the piezoelectric cantilever beam could only be effectively excited around its resonance frequency, the operating bandwidth of the directly-coupled wind energy harvesters was usually limited to a certain range. In particular, the piezoelectric cantilever beams would be easily damaged due to large and bidirectional deformation under the unexpected high-speed wind. However, very few studies have been reported on the reliability and environmental adaptability of VIV-based PWEHs. In view of this, it is necessary to design a novel structural scheme to improve the above weaknesses of the traditional VIV-based PWEHs.

Unlike the most existing VIV-based PWEHs where piezoelectric beams interacted directly with the airflow, wind energy harvesting from vortex-induced vibration of a composite piezoelectric transducer embedded in a cylindrical shell is explored for the first time. So a novel non-contact vortex-induced vibration-based piezoelectric wind energy harvester (abbreviated as NC-PWEH) using an indirectly excited piezoelectric transducer is presented in this paper. Meanwhile, to further enhance the reliability of the presented NC-PWEH, a pre-bending vibrator subjected to unidirectional compressive stress was employed to construct the composite piezoelectric transducer. It was also different from most previous VIV-based PWEHs where the piezoelectric vibrators underwent both the compressive stress and tensile stress simultaneously. Furthermore, the NC-PWEH has a good designability, where it could easily adapt to different wind speed by adjusting structural parameters like cylindrical shell mass and transducer mass. The configuration and principle of the NC-PWEH was introduced and a prototype PWEH was fabricated to verify the feasibility by the experimental wind-speed responses. The influence of wind speed and several key structural parameters like shell mass and transducer mass on the performance in terms of the wind speed bandwidth, voltage output and power output of the NC-PWEH was tested and analyzed.

sections.heading: 2.Structure and working principle of the NC-PWEH
sections.text:
The main objective of this work is to offer an alternative solution to overcome the shortcoming caused by direct interaction between the piezoelectric elements and the airflow for the existing VIV-based PWEHs so as to improve the reliability and environmental adaptability. Consequently, the piezoelectric transducer is placed in the hollow cylindrical shell and then indirectly excited by the shell subjected to VIV to vibrate and generate electric energy and thus a non-contact VIV-based PWEH is constructed. Fig. 1 shows a structure schematic of the proposed NC-PWEH. It consists of a pre-bending piezoelectric vibrator, a cylindrical shell, an added cantilever mass, an added shell mass, two supports and some springs. Among them, the combination of two pre-bending piezoelectric vibrators and the added cantilever mass is defined as the composite piezoelectric transducer. Besides, the pre-bending piezoelectric vibrator is composed of two (upper and lower) piezoelectric cantilever beams (consisting of piezoelectric plate and metal substrate plate) with a certain bending curvature and a copper sheet.

As shown in Fig. 1, the fixed end of the piezoelectric transducer is installed inside the cylinder shell as well as the added cantilever mass is located at the free end of the transducer. Some added shell mass is attached on the inner wall of the shell. The two external ends of the cylindrical shell are fixed on the support via four springs. Thus, the cylindrical shell is horizontally suspended and placed in the direction of incoming airflow.

![](images/f84ad222579e3f539e53f4af5928318b965c780c056d3334742f01812b8cfbe2.jpg)  
Fig. 1. Schematic illustration of the NC-PWEH.

Fig. 2 shows the working principle of the NC-PWEH. According to fluid dynamics theory, as the wind flows over the cylindrical shell, the periodic vortices shedding from the edge of the cylindrical shell is in a wide range of Reynolds numbers [32]. As shown in Fig. 2(a), the generated vortices induce a periodic lift force on the cylindrical shell, and thus the cylindrical shell is subjected to a longitudinal vibration. Then the added cantilever mass will be forced to vibrate upwards and downwards under the longitudinal vibration, meanwhile, the copper sheet also produces a swinging motion along the moving direction of the cantilever mass. As a result, the pre-bending piezoelectric vibrator further bends and generates electric energy under the excitation of the copper sheet. It is worth noting that both piezoelectric plates in the upper and lower sides will be respectively excited when the transducer mass vibrates for a working cycle. So twice electrical outputs are generated by the transducer. Fig. 2(b) illustrates schematically the force analysis of the piezoelectric transducer. It demonstrates that the piezoelectric elements only undergo the unidirectional compressive stress during the whole working process of NC-PWEH. It is very different from the most existing working mode of piezoelectric vibrators subjected to both the compressive stress and tensile stress simultaneously. Then it would be very likely to lead to the fatigue damage of the piezoelectric vibrators under the long-term alternating loads. It is well known that the compressive strength of PZT $\mathrm { \hbar } > 5 1 7 \mathrm { M P a } _ { \mathrm { \hbar } }$ is much higher than its tensile strength $( { \sim } 7 5 . 8 ~ \mathrm { M P a } )$ [33]. The reduction in tensile stress will extend the life time of the piezoelectric plate, reduce material replacement costs and improve application potential.

Most importantly, unlike most exsiting PWEHs where the piezoelectric elements are directly exposed to the wind, this paper focuses on wind energy recovery from vortex-induced vibration of a composite piezoelectric transducer embedded in a circular cylinder. Because the piezoelectric transducer is sealed in the cylindrical bluff body, the energy conversion in the non-contact PWEH is performed twice, namely the fluid kinetic energy vibration energy of the cylindrical shell vibration energy of the added cantilever mass electric energy. So the non-contact PWEH implements the energy conversion using an indirect interaction between the wind and piezoelectric transducer. Moreover, another benefit accompanied by the new design and configuration is its good designability because the non-contact PWEH can easily adapt to different wind speed by adjusting structural parameters like shell mass and transducer mass. The sealing measure is used to avoid the erosive and destructive effects of fluids on piezoelectric materials. So the design and working principle of the NC-PWEH determine that it can not only be utilized to harvest the wind energy, but also scavenge liquid energy and vibration energy. In short, it demonstrates that the NC-PWEH has relatively high reliability, good designability and excellent environmental adaptability.

sections.heading: 3. Fabrication and experiments
sections.text:
In order to verify the feasibility of the design and examine the influence of the wind speed $( \nu )$ , the cylindrical shell mass $( M _ { 1 } )$ and the piezoelectric transducer mass $\left( M _ { 2 } \right)$ on the output performance of the NC-PWEH, a prototype of NC-PWEH is fabricated and the experimental setup for testing is presented, as shown in Fig. 4. And the physical and schematic diagrams of the testing system are shown in Fig. 4 (ab) and Fig. 4 (c), respectively. The material properties and geometric dimensions of the prototype are illustrated in Table 1. Moreover, some important geometric parameters, such as lengths, diameters, etc., are also marked in Fig. 4(c). As for the testing system, a commercial centrifugal air blower was placed in front of the prototype to generate air flow in a desirable wind speed, and the wind speed can be continuously controllable via the frequency converter according to our working convenience. An anemometer was used to measure the wind speed, and thus the numerical relationship between wind speed and frequency of the converter could be established. The tuning frequencies of the frequency converter ranged from $_ { 0 \mathrm { ~ H z ~ } }$ to $5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ with $_ { 1 \mathrm { ~ H z ~ } }$ step. The generated voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ was observed by a digital oscilloscope (model DS5042M). Similar to most previous works, the peak-to-peak voltage was directly recorded as the output voltage of NC-PWEH, namely the generated voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ . The vibration amplitude of the cylindrical shell was measured by a scanning laser vibrometer (model PSV-500) after a reflective film was glued on the surface of the shell. An adjustable resistor was used to provide desired external load resistance. An electronic scale was utilized to measure the cylindrical shell mass and piezoelectric transducer mass. All the experimental data was processed by the computer and visually presented in figures. In the process of follow-up tests, an air blower and a frequency converter were used to simulate the wind field environment, and the wind speed (v) was transformed from the frequency $( f _ { \mathrm { c } } )$ of the frequency converter. Therefore, it was necessary to obtain the relationship between $\nu$ and $f _ { \mathrm { c } }$ for facilitating the experiments. Based on the manuals of the blower and frequency changer, a linear relationship of $\nu = 0 . 8 f _ { \mathrm { c } }$ could be deduced. In order to validate the accuracy of the linear relationship, the wind speed of the air blower outlet was tested by an anemometer with the varying frequency range from $_ { 0 \mathrm { ~ H z } }$ to $5 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ of frequency converter, as shown in Fig. 5. As can be seen from Fig. 5, a good agreement between the theoretical prediction and experimental results is observed. The relative error between tested and theoretical wind speed is less than $3 \%$ and thus it can be ignored in following experiments. In addition, to ensure the stability of the wind speed, a short time interval is usually needed after each adjusting of the frequency converter in experiments.

sections.heading: 3.4. Comparison and discussion
sections.text:
Based on the principle of vortex-induced vibration, a novel noncontact piezoelectric wind energy harvester was presented to enhance the reliability and environmental adaptability in this paper. The combination of embedded transducer and pre-bending piezoelectric vibrator was a kind of novel structure design in terms of piezoelectric wind energy harvesters, where the wind-induced vibration energy conversion into electrical energy was realized without the direct contact between the piezoelectric elements and the wind. So, unlike previous most PWEHs where the piezoelectric elements were directly exposed to the wind, we presented the wind energy recovery from vortex-induced vibration of a composite piezoelectric transducer embedded in a circular cylinder. To verify the feasibility of the proposed principle and design, the theoretical and experimental studies were performed. Experimental results showed that the wind speed, shell mass and piezoelectric transducer mass exerted a strong impact on the vibration and power generation characteristics for the NC-PWEH. At first, the effects of the cylindrical shell mass on vibration behaviors and power generation characteristics were compared and analyzed. The maximum vibration displacement, the maximum open-circuit voltage and their corresponding wind speeds were extracted from Figs. 7 and 8, respectively. Then the comparison of effects of the shell mass can be further made, as depicted in Fig. 16. The comparison results indicated that the effects of the cylindrical shell mass on vibration behaviors and power generation characteristics were similar. Specifically, both the maximum displacement and peak voltage demonstrated a decreasing trend with the increasing shell mass. Under the optimal shell mass of $1 6 0 \ g _ { \mathrm { ; } }$ , the maximum values of displacement and voltage were $2 . 3 4 \mathrm { ~ m m }$ and $3 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively. The influence of shell mass was completely different from the influence of wind speed on voltage and displacement where they increased with the increasing wind speed. The reason of the above phenomenon was that the lift force on the cylindrical shell was increased with the increase of wind speed, which led to the increase of vibration displacement and the corresponding generated voltage. However, the driving capability of the lift force dropped with the enhancing cylindrical shell mass. Therefore, the maximum displacement would decrease with the rising cylindrical shell mass at similar wind speed. In short, the increase of cylindrical shell mass would reduce the maximum vibration displacement of cylindrical shell caused by the lift force. Meanwhile, the generated voltage would also be reduced with the increasing shell mass. ![](images/e22b3f2414dd0d3c6dc2150ef37258c2e3f8bfe1de4e794e1025db8c4a754b33.jpg) Fig. 14. Comparison of the bandwidth of wind speed at different shell mass $\left( M _ { 1 } \right)$ under the criterion voltage of ${ 5 . 0 \ V }$ . ![](images/9c587fbfe9bcda2d5d88c1565824dc79a8d44a6f24643e858f1ee6ea91476e3b.jpg) Fig. 16. Comparison of effects of the cylindrical shell mass on vibration characteristics and power generation characteristics of the NC-PWEH. Secondly, by extracting the maximum vibration displacement and peak voltage as well as their corresponding wind speed from Figs. 11 and 12, a comparison of effects of the piezoelectric transducer mass on vibration characteristics and power generation characteristics is illustrated in Fig. 17. The comparison results showed that the influence of the transducer mass on the vibration behaviors and power generation characteristics was also consistent. Specifically, the peak generated voltage and maximum vibration displacement of the NC-PWEH increased firstly and then decreased gradually with the increasing piezoelectric transducer mass. Basically, under the small-mass conditions, the influence on the power generation performance was greater than the effect on the vibration characteristics. So, the peak voltage would rapidly rise when transducer mass was increased from $4 5 ~ g$ to 65 g, whereas the optimal vibration displacement presented a very modest change with the varying transducer mass. Nevertheless, both the peak voltage and maximum displacement decreased significantly as the transducer mass was increased to $8 5 g$ , whereas there was only one peak in the range from $4 5 ~ g$ to $_ { 8 5 ~ g }$ , In contrast, the transducer mass had a very similar influence on the optimal vibration displacement and peak voltage, whereas the influence of the shell mass on them was quite different. It is worth noting that the cylindrical shell mass $( M _ { 1 } )$ brought a more significant effect on the vibration displacement than the piezoelectric transducer mass $\left( M _ { 2 } \right)$ by comparing the Figs. 16 and 17. The reason was that the testing range of the piezoelectric transducer mass was smaller than that of the shell mass, which was limited by the maximum allowable strain of the piezoelectric material. So, the piezoelectric transducer mass would not bring about too much change against the total mass of the NC-PWEH due to a much larger shell mass. In addition, both the vibration displacement and the generated voltage reached the maximum under a specific mass for the NC-PWEH. It meant the vibration characteristics were consistent with the power generation characteristics. In addition, because the inertia force (namely the excitation force of piezoelectric vibrators) was enhanced with the rising transducer mass, the piezoelectric vibrators could generate a rising deformation and electric output with the increasing transducer mass in a certain range. Nevertheless, when an excessive transducer mass was adopted, the prebending curvature of the upper piezoelectric plate would reduce and the vibration amplitude of the mass would also decrease under the same lift force. Accordingly, the generated voltage decreased with the reducing vibration amplitude. ![](images/ff76e457ad1e97ab1576f2d5d93293b5deb89ed1956035f717219a1e80515f0f.jpg) Fig. 17. Comparison of effects of the piezoelectric transducer mass on vibration characteristics and power generation characteristics of the NC-PWEH. Through the aforementioned experiments, it proved the feasibility of wind energy harvesting through the combination of a sealed cylindrical shell and an embedded pre-bending piezoelectric transducer. Because the piezoelectric transducer embedded in the cylindrical shell was indirectly excited to generate electric energy as well as a pre-bending PZT vibrator subjected to unidirectional compressive stress was used to construct the transducer, it was benefit for enhancing the reliability and environmental adaptability of PWEHs. Here, the maximum output power generated by a single piezoelectric beam in NC-PWEH was 1.438 mW in the experiments. Therefore, the NC-PWEH would produce about $2 . 8 7 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ because of symmetrical configuration of piezoelectric vibrators. According to Ref. [42], it demonstrated that the wind energy harvester with the electric output of 8.8 V, 0.155 mW and $9 1 7 ~ \mathrm { u J }$ was able to power the radio frequency (RF) transmitter to transmit 5 digital words of 12-bit information during the transmission period of $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m s } }$ . Basically, the electrical energy generated by the proposed NC-PWEH could meet the self-powered requirements of most MEMS sensor systems and wireless electronic devices. Moreover, the electric energy produced by the NC-PWEH could be firstly accumulated in a capacitor. Then the stored energy could be released to the RF transmitter via a trigger signal when the sufficient charges was accumulated in practical applications. A performance comparison among different vortexinduced vibration piezoelectric wind energy harvesters is summarized in Table 8. In comparison, the NC-PWEH harvester presented a relatively high reliability and good environmental adaptability. The reliability of the NC-PWEH could be reflected from the following facts, for instance, it could normally work in the wind speed range of $0 { - } 4 0 \ \mathrm { m } . s ^ { - 1 }$ , the sealed cylindrical shell could isolate the erosion effect of the fluid on the piezoelectric material, the pre-bending structure made the piezoelectric plate only undergo the unidirectional compressive stress. The good environmental adaptability could be presented in term of different application environments. The structural characteristics of NC-PWEH determined that it could harvest not only the wide-range $( 0 { - } 4 0 ~ \mathrm { m } . s ^ { - 1 } )$ wind energy, but also water-flow energy, and meanwhile available ambient vibration energy. Furthermore, the vibration characteristics, the bandwidth of wind speed and the power generation performance of NC-PWEH could be improved with the increasing wind speed, increasing transducer mass and the decreasing shell mass. Thus, it demonstrated that the NC-PWEH had high reliability and strong environmental adaptability. Not only the novel structure of NC-PWEH could provide a reference for improving the reliability and environmental adaptability of VIV-based PWEHs, but also a galloping PWEH with high reliability and good environmental adaptability could be constructed by transforming the cylindrical shell into a rectangular or triangular bluff body. sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: A novel non-contact piezoelectric wind energy harvester excited by vortex-induced vibration (NC-PWEH) is proposed to enhance the reliability and environmental adaptability in this paper, where the combination of embedded transducer and pre-bending piezoelectric vibrator was adopted to harvest wind-induced vibration energy for the first time. The wind energy recovery from VIV of a composite piezoelectric transducer composed of two pre-bending vibrators and an added cantilever mass and embedded in a circular cylinder was explored in theory and experiment. To verify the feasibility of the presented NC-PWEH, the vibration characteristics and power generation performance were investigated by theoretical analysis and experiments. And a prototype was fabricated and tested in terms of vibration displacement of the shell, wind speed bandwidth and output power. The experimental results indicated that the cylindrical shell mass, the piezoelectric transducer mass, and wind speed brought significant effects on the vibration displacement, output voltage and power. Also, it demonstrated that the vibration characteristics of the NC-PWEH were consistent with the voltage output characteristics. Specifically, both the vibration characteristics and power generation performance could be improved by increasing the piezoelectric transducer mass to an appropriate value (about $6 5 g \dot { }$ within the tested wind speed range. The bandwidth of wind speed (BOws) could be broadened by adjusting the transducer mass and the shell mass. The maximum BOwS reached $3 4 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m } . s ^ { - 1 }$ under the transducer mass of $6 5 \ { \tt g } \mathrm { _ { \mathrm { 3 } } }$ , where it accounted for $8 5 . 8 \%$ of the whole tested wind-speed range of $4 0 . 0 \ m . s ^ { - 1 }$ . Furthermore, there was an optimal load resistance of $3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to maximize the output power. For a single piezoelectric vibrator, the maximum output power of $1 . 4 3 8 \mathrm { \ m W }$ was recorded at the transducer mass of $6 5 g$ and the wind speed of 40.0 $\mathbf { m } . s ^ { - 1 }$ . The experimental process also implied that the novel NC-PWEH might be employed to scavenge the wind energy, water-flow energy, and ambient vibration energy. The proposed design could not only be beneficial for improving the reliability and environmental adaptability of VIV-based PWEHs, but also provide a reference for galloping PWEHs.
